content: New systematic reviews or updates to existing systematic reviews were conducted to evaluate the effects of interventions, including screening tests, on health outcomes and to assess the accuracy of screening tests in the general population of women and in women living with HIV. Four PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) questions were developed, each accompanied by systematic reviews, evidence-to-decision (EtD) tables, and corresponding recommendations or good-practice statements. These questions addressed interventions and test accuracy for both the general population of women and women living with HIV. Evidence reviews were conducted to assess interventions for the general population of women, the accuracy of triage tests, and interventions for women living with HIV. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) handbook materials and supplementary materials were used to support these reviews. Specific EtD tables were created for PICO questions related to the general population and women living with HIV, covering topics such as the age to initiate and end screening, follow-up strategies after screening or treatment, and treatment within specific timeframes. An individual patient data meta-analysis (IPD-MA) was performed to analyze age-specific data for cervical cancer and cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) in women living with HIV. Authors of studies identified in the systematic review were contacted to provide datasets, which were reviewed, aligned, and combined. Random-effects models were used to calculate predicted probabilities for cervical screening outcomes based on age, HIV status, and other factors. Mathematical modeling was conducted using the Policy1-Cervix platform, a validated dynamic model of HPV transmission, vaccination, natural history, cancer survival, screening, diagnosis, and treatment. This model was applied to predict outcomes in women across 78 lowand middle-income countries. A specific HIV-HPV model was used to evaluate cervical cancer outcomes among women living with HIV in Tanzania, where sufficient local data on cervical cancer control and HIV burden were available. Baseline assumptions included 70% screening attendance and 90% follow-up compliance, with outcomes assessed over the lifetime of birth cohorts eligible for screening from 2030 onward. A systematic review of values and preferences was conducted to understand the perspectives of end-users, healthcare providers, and stakeholders regarding cervical cancer screening and treatment. An anonymous survey was distributed to women aged 15 years and older, with responses analyzed to inform the guideline development process. The survey was approved by the WHO Ethics Review Committee and promoted through various channels, including civil society groups and WHO advisory groups. Feasibility, acceptability, resource use, and equity considerations were assessed through a survey of the Guideline Development Group (GDG) members. The survey evaluated implementation considerations for priority algorithms, including demand generation, access to screening, workforce training, infrastructure development, and integration with other health services. The GDG also considered the perspectives of various stakeholder groups, including health authorities, professional societies, healthcare providers, community health workers, and clients. The development of recommendations involved virtual GDG meetings, during which evidence-to-decision tables were discussed. These tables summarized evidence on benefits, harms, values, preferences, resource use, feasibility, equity, and acceptability. GDG members provided input through email and during meetings, and consensus was reached on all recommendations. Strong recommendations were made when the benefits of an intervention clearly outweighed the harms, while conditional recommendations were made when the benefits probably outweighed the harms. The WHO recommendations aim to improve cervical cancer screening coverage and outcomes, set quality standards, and reduce cervical cancer mortality. Bridging strategies may be needed to transition from existing screening infrastructure to the implementation of these recommendations. Population-based screening and treatment strategies are encouraged, and programs should ensure that women who screen positive receive appropriate follow-up and treatment. Screening and treatment should also be provided to transgender men, non-binary individuals, and intersex individuals with a cervix, with more data needed for these populations. WHO recognizes the importance of high-quality screening tests approved by regulatory agencies and emphasizes the need for strong links between different levels of healthcare services to ensure continuity and completeness of care. Future stepwise implementation guidelines will support the adaptation and scale-up of these recommendations.
